strengths: The paper addresses an important and comparatively underexplored problem: inference-time safety alignment for large audio-language models. The paired harmful/lexically similar safe evaluation is particularly useful because ordinary benign benchmarks can conceal over-refusal.
SARSteer is simple, training-free, and computationally plausible: it derives a refusal direction from a textual prompt and removes components aligned with a PCA-estimated safe subspace.

The evaluation has meaningful breadth, covering Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, and Qwen2-Audio-Base; four harmful-query benchmarks; paired helpfulness tests; and AirBench general utility. The ablations examine both proposed components, sample count, steering strength, PCA rank, prompt choice, and refusal-direction construction.

The reported results show a promising safety–helpfulness trade-off. On Qwen2-Audio, SARSteer reduces Figstep-audio ASR from 51.6% to 10.8% while increasing BRR from 70.2% to 79.95%. On Kimi-Audio, it raises Figstep BRR from 61.4% to 88.8%, although its ASR is worse than AdaShield there.

The manuscript is generally organized and discloses its use of LLMs in writing, figure preparation, and initial code development. weaknesses: The central geometric explanation is not established. A two-dimensional t-SNE visualization cannot demonstrate the existence or absence of a valid linear steering path, preserve global distances, or justify the strong conclusion that speech activations are fundamentally unsuitable for steering. Indeed, separation of harmful and safe audio representations could make a discriminative direction easier to identify. The poor MDSteer results could instead arise from layer choice, direction normalization, or coefficient tuning, none of which is adequately controlled.

The claimed theoretical intuition is circular and technically unsupported. Appendix A.4 assumes that harmful-input gradients align positively with the projected refusal vector and that safe activations lying in the PCA subspace implies their refusal-logit gradients also lie in that subspace. The latter does not follow: activation location and local output gradient are different objects. Consequently, PCA projection of safe activation variance provides no guarantee that a constant intervention will selectively affect harmful inputs.

Helpfulness is measured primarily by keyword-based BRR, not by whether benign questions receive correct and useful answers. The keyword list includes extremely broad strings such as “avoid,” “Hello!,” “As an,” and “It is important to note,” creating substantial false-positive risk. Because SARSteer is explicitly derived from “I cannot assist with that,” its evaluation is also unusually coupled to the refusal phrases used by this metric. AirBench does not repair this issue for the specially constructed borderline-safe examples.

The experimental comparison does not isolate the relevant trade-off fairly. Steering baselines reuse alpha=0.1 despite potentially very different vector norms and receive no reported tuning, while SARSteer's alpha directly controls the trade-off. There are no safety–helpfulness curves, matched-BRR or matched-ASR comparisons, confidence intervals, repeated samples, or significance tests. Hyperparameter selection and whether the reported Figstep evaluation set was used during tuning are also unclear.

Robustness and external validity are limited. Most evaluation audio is generated from text with one TTS system and a fixed accompanying instruction, with no study of speakers, accents, recording conditions, natural speech, ASR ambiguity, or adaptive attacks aware of the defense. Only 200 of 1,495 AJailBench examples are sampled, without a released index or uncertainty estimate. Thus claims of robustness and modality-wide conclusions are too broad.

Reproducibility is inadequate for reliably rebuilding the results. The paper does not provide code or generated data, random seeds, decoding parameters, exact model checkpoints, the DeepSeek model/version and purification prompt, human validation of the purportedly safe rewrites, precise intervention hooks, or clear layer-selection details. Reliance on an externally versioned proprietary OpenAI TTS service further complicates exact reproduction.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: refusal-direction activation steering and PCA projection are known ingredients, with novelty mainly in their combination and application to audio models. The assertion that this is the first inference-time LALM defense is not supported by a sufficiently comprehensive comparison with generic input/output moderation, safety classifiers, self-evaluation, or other modality-agnostic inference defenses.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: Section 5.3 says the best method has “high ASR” even though lower ASR is the stated objective, and several claims use causal or universal language unsupported by the evidence. There is also no substantive limitations or ethics discussion addressing residual unsafe behavior, false reassurance in deployment, bias introduced by synthetic safe rewrites, or dual-use implications. These omissions matter for a safety paper, although the disclosed LLM assistance itself is not a concern.

strengths: Significance: Safety alignment for audio-language models is timely and comparatively underexplored, and jointly measuring harmful-query refusal, borderline-safe over-refusal, and general utility is a useful framing.

Method: SARSteer is computationally lightweight and training-free. Its combination of a text-derived refusal direction with projection away from principal components of benign activations is simple enough to deploy on open-weight models.

Evaluation breadth: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/586e9669cca94f6fae196b794f197035/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} evaluates Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio on four safety datasets, paired benign examples, and AirBench, with component and hyperparameter ablations plus a Qwen2-Audio-Base experiment.

Empirical results: On Qwen2-Audio, SARSteer substantially reduces Figstep-audio ASR from 51.6% to 10.8% while raising BRR from 70.2% to 79.95%. On Kimi-Audio it raises Figstep-audio BRR from 61.4% to 88.8%, suggesting that the intervention may offer a useful safety–over-refusal trade-off.
Presentation: The paper is generally organized clearly, defines its metrics and intervention explicitly, and includes an algorithm outline and descriptions of the constructed datasets.
weaknesses: Soundness—unsupported mechanistic conclusion: Figure 2 uses a two-dimensional t-SNE visualization to infer that audio activations have no shared subspace, that harmful-to-safe directions become noisy, and ultimately that speech activations “cannot serve as a feasible operating space for safety steering.” t-SNE cannot establish any of these geometric claims; visible separation could even make a linear direction easier to identify. No quantitative separability, subspace-overlap, intrinsic-dimensionality, or causal intervention analysis supports this central explanation.

Soundness—the PCA argument is asserted rather than demonstrated: high-variance principal components of benign activations are not necessarily a “safe semantic subspace.” The appendix’s mathematical intuition assumes, without evidence, precisely the input-dependent gradient alignments needed for the method to work. Under a fixed local linear classifier, adding the same vector produces the same logit shift for safe and harmful inputs, so input selectivity does not follow merely from orthogonalizing against benign activation variance.

Evaluation validity: BRR relies on brittle substring matching. Its refusal list includes broad phrases such as “Hello!”, “As an,” “avoid,” and “It is important to note,” which can occur in helpful answers, while refusals using other wording can be missed. There is no validation against human labels or a robust refusal classifier. Because BRR is the principal evidence that SARSteer avoids over-refusal, this is a material weakness.

Dataset validity and realism: The borderline-safe examples are automatically rewritten by DeepSeek-R1, but the paper reports no human verification that they are genuinely benign, meaning-preserving, natural, or matched in difficulty. Most evaluation audio is synthesized from text through a single unspecified OpenAI TTS configuration. There is no evaluation across speakers, accents, languages, environmental noise, recording conditions, or natural user speech, substantially limiting the claimed relevance to audio safety.

Baseline fairness is unclear: competing steering methods are assigned the same coefficient alpha=0.1 despite potentially very different vector norms and optimal scales, with no per-baseline validation or trade-off curves. The prompt baselines are minimally adapted vision defenses, and a direct simple refusal-prompt baseline corresponding to the text used by SARSteer is missing. Thus the experiments do not establish superiority over well-tuned alternatives.

Experimental selection and uncertainty are inadequately documented: alpha and k appear to be analyzed on Figstep-audio itself, but no validation split or hyperparameter-selection protocol is given. Results are single point estimates without repeated sampling, confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity to the randomly chosen 100 alignment pairs and 200 AJailBench examples. Small score differences, especially on AirBench, therefore cannot support comparative claims.

Limited evidence for robustness: The intervention is evaluated against fixed benchmarks, not adaptive attacks designed with knowledge of the steering vector. Several tasks are already nearly saturated—for example, AdvBench-audio ASR is 2.88% or 0% without defense—and on Kimi-Audio SARSteer is worse than AdaShield on harmfulness across multiple datasets. The evidence supports a potentially useful operating point, not the paper’s broad robustness and generality claims.

Originality is moderate: the method combines established mean-difference activation steering with a standard PCA orthogonal projection. Applying this combination to audio-language models is new in context, but the conceptual advance is limited, especially because the proposed interpretation of the projection is not validated.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code or dataset-release commitment is stated, and essential details are absent or ambiguous, including exact checkpoints, insertion layers and hooks, whether all layers are modified simultaneously, activation centering/normalization, PCA preprocessing, decoding settings, random seeds, TTS voice/settings, purification prompts, and baseline prompts. Algorithm 1 also writes Q'=(Q+p), obscuring how audio and text components are combined.

Presentation and limitations: The text sometimes overstates evidence and contains inconsistencies—for example, Section 5.3 describes the preferred variant as having “high ASR” even though lower ASR is better. The paper has no substantive limitations or ethics discussion addressing false refusals, demographic and accent bias, automated-label failure, synthetic-audio limitations, adaptive adversaries, or the dual-use implications of audio jailbreak research. These omissions are important for a safety paper.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/22fefb5c1abd4b66b7cad52e0591614d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important and underexplored problem: inference-time safety alignment for audio-language models. Adapting refusal steering to this modality and explicitly considering borderline-safe speech are useful contributions.

The proposed combination of text-derived refusal steering and PCA-based safe-space ablation is simple, computationally plausible, and reasonably original in the LALM setting. The paired harmful/safe construction is also a valuable evaluation idea because ordinary benign benchmarks can conceal over-refusal.

The empirical coverage is comparatively broad: two instruction-tuned LALMs, a base model, four harmfulness benchmarks, two paired helpfulness benchmarks, AirBench utility evaluation, and a small text-LLM transfer study. In Table 2, SARSteer substantially reduces Qwen2-Audio ASR on Figstep-audio from 51.6% to 10.8% while raising BRR from 70.2% to 79.95%; on Kimi-Audio it raises Figstep BRR from 61.4% to 88.8%.

Ablations separate the refusal-vector and safe-space components, while sensitivity studies examine sample count, steering strength, PCA rank, and alternative refusal prompts. These experiments support the practical usefulness of the full construction, even if they do not completely establish its proposed mechanism.

The paper is clearly organized and visually polished. Definitions, algorithms, datasets, baseline adaptations, and refusal phrases are documented in the appendix, and the authors disclose their use of LLM assistance.
weaknesses: The claim that speech activations cannot provide a feasible steering space is substantially overdrawn. It rests mainly on two-dimensional t-SNE plots for Qwen2-Audio and the failure of two adapted baselines. t-SNE cannot establish linear separability, absence of a shared subspace, or impossibility of steering. Moreover, all raw steering directions use the same alpha=0.1 despite potentially different vector norms; normalization or independently validated strengths are necessary for a fair comparison.

The theoretical explanation for safe-space ablation is not sound as written. PCA of benign hidden activations identifies high-variance activation directions, but this does not imply that gradients of a refusal logit for benign inputs lie in that subspace. The appendix assumes this key relationship rather than deriving or measuring it. It also states that a refusal logit is high for regular safe inputs because the model produces normal answers, which conflicts with the stated meaning of that logit.

The central helpfulness evidence relies on brittle substring matching. Phrases such as "avoid," "refrain," "Hello!," "As an," and "It is important to note" can appear in legitimate benign answers, so BRR may confound refusal with ordinary language. The LLM-generated safe counterparts are not reported as human-validated. Human evaluation, a validated refusal classifier, and category-level false-positive analysis would materially strengthen the over-refusal claim.

Results are presented as single point estimates without confidence intervals, repeated seeds, significance testing, or a documented validation protocol for selecting alpha, PCA rank, layers, and prompts. Sensitivity curves appear to use the evaluation benchmark itself, creating possible test-set tuning. The random 200-example AJailBench subset is also insufficiently specified.

External validity remains limited. Most data are text benchmarks converted through one unspecified OpenAI TTS configuration and a fixed textual wrapper, so robustness to natural speakers, accents, recording conditions, paraphrases, conversational context, non-speech audio, and adaptive attacks is unclear. Evaluation on only two closely studied LALMs further limits the broad claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code or dataset availability statement, and essential details such as exact injection hooks/layers, whether PCA is centered, vector normalization, decoding parameters, TTS voice/settings, safe-query generation prompt and model version, random seeds, and inference-time memory/latency are missing.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion. It should discuss false refusals in consequential voice applications, evaluator and synthetic-data bias, adaptive circumvention, dual-use risks of releasing harmful audio, privacy implications for real speech, and the fact that activation access restricts deployment to white-box models. These omissions reduce confidence but do not presently constitute an irresolvable ethical concern.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an audio-safety paper: it covers multiple harmful and paired-safe benchmarks, general utility, five LALM families, five random seeds, natural-speech transformations, signal perturbations, and audio-converted PAIR/GCG attacks. The main results show a credible safety-utility improvement, particularly on Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio.

Evaluation: The paired harmful-safe construction exposes over-refusal that aggregate benign benchmarks such as AirBench can conceal. Reporting ASR, safe refusal behavior, BRR, and general utility provides a more informative picture than harmful-query refusal alone.

Evaluation quality: The 500-example blinded human study reports 90.8% agreement and Cohen's kappa of 0.811 with the automated safety judge, while identifying its conservative bias. Multi-seed results also suggest that the main improvements are not sampling artifacts.

Originality: Combining text-derived refusal steering with removal of principal directions estimated from safe audio activations is a simple but novel adaptation of activation steering to LALMs. The modality-specific empirical investigation and paired audio datasets are useful additions to a sparsely studied area.

Significance: An inference-time intervention requiring only 100 calibration pairs could be practically useful when model fine-tuning is unavailable. Results on newer models indicate some cross-architecture portability, although the gains are not uniformly large.

Presentation and ethics: The paper is generally organized clearly, supplies an algorithm and extensive appendices, acknowledges residual safety concerns, and includes an impact statement recommending continued evaluation and human oversight.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central mechanistic explanation is not established. Separation in t-SNE plots and low CKA between harmful and safe audio representations do not imply that audio lacks a valid linear steering direction or a shared subspace. Consequently, the strong claim that speech activations cannot serve as a feasible steering space is unsupported by the presented analyses.

Soundness: The PCA argument conflates directions of high variance among safe activations with a semantic safe subspace. No result proves that removing these directions preserves benign behavior or isolates harmful features. The local-linear analysis assumes the crucial alignments it is meant to explain—for example, that gradients for safe inputs lie mainly in the PCA subspace—rather than deriving or measuring them.

Soundness: Appendix B.13 does not validate the theoretical mechanism. The proposed proxy, the inner product between the steering vector and an activation, is not a proxy for the claimed logit change, which depends on the output gradient's inner product with the steering vector. Its negative values and modest effect size therefore cannot substantiate selective activation on harmful samples.

Evaluation: BRR uses brittle phrase matching rather than semantic correctness or helpfulness. Benign paired prompts are automatically rewritten by DeepSeek and synthesized by TTS, but the manuscript reports no human validation of their safety, naturalness, lexical matching, or answer quality. A method could improve BRR by avoiding listed refusal phrases without actually giving useful safe answers.

Evaluation: Several robustness claims are overstated. The so-called adaptive PAIR/GCG attacks appear to be generated independently of SARSteer's intervention rather than optimized against the defended model. The PGD objective and optimization protocol are unspecified, and the natural-speech experiment uses synthetic augmentations rather than recordings from human speakers.

Evaluation and significance: Baseline coverage and fairness are incomplete. The audio-specific RRS method is deliberately trained on only 100 examples despite reportedly using 2,100 in its original setup, making its poor comparison inconclusive. ALMGuard is discussed but not evaluated, and inference-time latency or per-token overhead is not reported. On newer models, improvements are mixed—for example, SARSteer remains at 31.2% ASR on Qwen2.5-Omni and reduces Voxtral BRR below the undefended model.

Reproducibility: Important details are missing, including exact checkpoints and revisions, decoding settings, preprocessing and normalization, layer/token intervention hooks for each architecture, prompts used to create safe pairs and judge outputs, TTS settings, PGD/PAIR/GCG configurations, and inference overhead. The abstract says code and data are released but provides no accessible link in the submitted manuscript.

Presentation: Some mathematical and experimental descriptions are ambiguous or erroneous. Equation 14 appears to project the mean-safe vector onto the refusal vector while describing the reverse operation; centered PCA versus SVD is not clarified even though these should be closely related; and claims such as 'fundamental limitation,' 'principled,' and robustness across five attack categories exceed the evidence.

Limitations and ethics: The impact statement is positive but does not adequately discuss dual-use risks from releasing harmful audio prompts, privacy or licensing implications of the TTS and benchmark data, annotator recruitment and welfare, or failure modes under languages, accents, codecs, background noise, and genuinely defense-aware attacks. These omissions matter for a proposed safety defense.

Overall: The paper has a promising method and substantial experiments, but unreliable helpfulness measurement, under-specified robustness tests, incomplete reproducibility, and unsupported causal/geometric claims currently prevent others from confidently building on its central conclusions. Major revision is needed, so the weaknesses outweigh the merits.

strengths: Significance: Audio-language model safety is timely and practically important, and the paper usefully emphasizes that defenses should be evaluated for both harmful-query refusal and over-refusal on lexically similar benign requests.

Originality: Combining a text-derived refusal direction with projection away from a PCA-estimated benign subspace is a simple, potentially useful inference-time adaptation of activation steering to audio-language models.

Empirical breadth: The study reports results for multiple audio-language models, harmful-query benchmarks, a general-utility benchmark, recent models, natural-speech variations, several attacks, ablations, and five random seeds. The large reductions reported on Qwen2-Audio are promising.

Presentation: The main algorithm is easy to follow, the harmful/safe paired-data motivation is clearly explained, and the paper distinguishes harmfulness, borderline-safe helpfulness, and general utility rather than collapsing them into one metric.

The appendix includes a blinded human check of the harmful-response judge, hyperparameter analyses, and sample-level statistics, which are useful attempts to probe robustness and measurement reliability.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central geometric explanation is not established. A t-SNE plot cannot show that audio representations have “no shared subspace” or that audio-space steering is fundamentally infeasible. Likewise, lower CKA between paired harmful and safe audio representations neither proves non-steerability nor excludes confounds from utterance length, acoustics, or the generated safe rewrites. The manuscript turns correlations from two initial models into an overly broad causal claim.

Soundness: The theoretical account in Appendix A.4 is circular and contains a serious inconsistency. It states that benign inputs have a high “refusal logit,” although helpful benign behavior requires low refusal propensity. More fundamentally, membership of hidden activations in a PCA subspace does not imply that the input-dependent refusal-logit gradient lies in that subspace. Equations 18–21 assume precisely the gradient alignments needed for the desired conclusion and therefore do not justify why PCA ablation should selectively affect harmful inputs.

Soundness: Removing directions of greatest variance among safe activations is not intrinsically equivalent to preserving safe semantics. PCA is unsupervised, and the paper does not show that its components represent safety rather than topic, lexical, acoustic, or length variation. The proposed sample proxy δ=<v,h> is also not a faithful proxy for the claimed logit change α<w,v>, since h and the output gradient w are different objects. Both group means in Table 18 are negative and only 6% of harmful examples have positive δ, further weakening the stated interpretation.

Evaluation: The central helpfulness result relies on substring-based refusal detection containing extremely broad expressions such as “Hello!”, “As an,” “avoid,” and “It is important to note.” This can misclassify ordinary helpful answers. No human evaluation validates BRR or the quality/correctness of safe-query answers; the reported human study only checks safe-versus-unsafe judgments for the ASR evaluator. Consequently, the main claim of mitigating over-refusal is not convincingly measured.

Evaluation: The paired safe queries are generated by an LLM and converted with TTS, but their benignness, naturalness, semantic fidelity, and lexical matching are not human-validated. The principal experiments therefore may reflect artifacts of one synthetic construction pipeline. The natural-speech experiment is small and uses a benchmark with synthetic characteristics; its baseline ASR is already only 1.5%, making it weak evidence for deployment robustness.

Comparisons: Baseline steering methods use the same raw coefficient α=0.1 despite potentially very different vector norms, and there is no per-baseline validation or norm matching. This can make the vanilla steering baselines arbitrarily weak or destructive. The RRS comparison is explicitly trained with only 100 examples although its original setting uses 2,100, so it does not support a meaningful superiority claim over training-based defenses. Stronger guard-model, classifier-gated, output-filtering, and appropriately tuned activation-steering baselines are missing.

Robustness evidence is under-specified and sometimes misleading. The PGD objective, step count, step size, intelligibility constraints, decoding configuration, and attack adaptation are absent. Noise and PGD substantially lower the undefended ASR relative to clean audio, apparently by damaging the input, while PAIR/GCG use only 50 examples. These experiments do not substantiate broad robustness against adaptive attackers.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported scope. The abstract’s code-release link is blank, and essential details such as exact intervention layers, whether all layers are modified simultaneously, activation/token selection, PCA centering, decoding settings, TTS voices and parameters, safe-query generation prompt, baseline prompts/configuration, model checkpoints, and attack implementations are missing or ambiguous. Runtime numbers are also given without hardware or a precise accounting protocol.

Presentation and limitations: The writing is readable but repeatedly overstates limited evidence using terms such as “fundamental limitation,” “principled,” and “robust.” There is no substantive limitations section discussing synthetic-data dependence, white-box access, inference overhead, evaluator error, language/voice coverage, or possible adaptive circumvention.

Research ethics: Although an impact statement is provided, the manuscript gives no meaningful release-risk analysis for harmful audio datasets, no access or redaction plan, and no description of annotator recruitment, expertise, compensation, consent, or adjudication for the human evaluation. These omissions are material for a safety paper involving harmful-content annotation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: inference-time safety alignment for large audio-language models. Text-derived refusal steering combined with safe-subspace ablation is a simple, practically useful contribution with moderate originality. The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: it covers several LALMs, four principal safety benchmarks, paired borderline-safe examples, AirBench utility, recent-model extensions, five-seed stability tests, alternative prompts and decompositions, natural-speech variations, and adaptive attacks.

On Qwen2-Audio, the main results are compelling: SARSteer reduces Figstep ASR from 51.6% to 10.8% and AJailBench ASR from 48.76% to 18.0%, while improving Figstep BRR from 70.2% to 79.95% and preserving AirBench performance. Results also transfer across datasets despite constructing the steering vectors from only 100 Figstep-audio pairs.

The paired harmful–safe evaluation is valuable. It reveals over-refusal that aggregate benign benchmarks conceal and makes the safety–utility trade-off more visible than reporting attack success alone.

Presentation is clear and well organized. The method, objectives, algorithm, ablations, evaluator validation, and impact statement are easy to follow. Human evaluation of 500 responses, with 90.8% agreement and Cohen's kappa of 0.811, materially strengthens confidence in the ASR evaluator.

The work has positive societal motivation and evaluates attacks defensively. The impact statement appropriately recommends continued evaluation and human oversight, and I found no material ethical issue that should block acceptance.
weaknesses: The paper's mechanistic explanation is not established. Separation in a t-SNE plot does not imply that audio representations have “no shared subspace” or that a valid steering path cannot exist; indeed, separability can make a mean-difference direction easier to identify. The reported CKA values quantify representational differences but likewise do not demonstrate the claimed causal explanation for steering failure.

The PCA argument is substantially stronger than its mathematical support. Top principal components of centered benign activations capture directions of high benign variance, not necessarily “safe semantics.” Removing those components from a refusal vector does not ensure that the residual is harmfulness-specific. Appendix A.4 also infers properties of the refusal gradient w from the location of activations h, which does not follow, while Appendix B.13 uses <v,h> as a proxy for w^T v without justifying a relationship between h and w. These sections should be framed as hypotheses or intuitions rather than validation.

The principal helpfulness result relies on a brittle substring-based refusal detector containing broad phrases such as “Hello!”, “As an,” “avoid,” and “It is important to note.” Such phrases can occur in helpful answers, and the 500-sample human study validates the separate LLM-based ASR judge rather than this matching-based BRR measure. Human validation of harmful and benign refusal labels is needed because mitigation of over-refusal is central to the contribution.

Performance is less uniformly strong than the prose suggests. On Qwen3-Omni and Voxtral, SARSteer provides only modest ASR improvements while slightly reducing BRR relative to no defense; on MiDashengLM it lowers Figstep BRR. The fine-tuning comparison is also not fully informative because RRS is trained with only 100 examples rather than the 2,100 used in its original setup.

The evaluation data are dominated by synthetic TTS speech, and the LLM-purified benign counterparts are not reported as human-verified. The natural-speech experiment uses a setting where the undefended ASR is already only 1.5%, so it offers little evidence about difficult real-speaker conditions, accents, recording noise, or conversational speech.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract's code/data-release sentence has no URL, and important details such as the exact layer-injection implementation, dataset split identifiers, purification prompts, TTS configuration, generation settings, evaluation prompts, hardware, and human-annotation protocol are missing or only partially specified.

The ethics discussion could more explicitly address safeguards for releasing harmful audio prompts and annotator exposure to harmful generated content. These are remediable documentation issues rather than acceptance-blocking concerns.

Overall, this is a useful, empirically promising contribution whose breadth and practical relevance justify a weak accept. The score is limited to 4 because the core causal interpretation and PCA justification are overstated, and the main over-refusal evidence lacks human validation.
